newsitem.title: USA: Ford studying structure of new parts unit.
newsitem.headline: Ford studying structure of new parts unit.

text.p: Ford Motor Co's decision to organize its components business into a separate unit could involve both expanding into new areas and shedding existing product lines, Chairman Alex Trotman said Thursday.
Trotman told reporters at a briefing at Ford World Headquarters that the company is in the early stages of evaluating what it wants the new unit, called Automotive Products Operations, to look like.
"We really don't know how it's going to roll out over the next year or two," Trotman said.
"Although we're convinced it will be better than the format we were in yesterday, we can't give you any details because we don't know what those are," he said.

Ford, as part of a sweeping reorganization and management re-alignment, combined four component divisions into the new parts unit. Those are the Automotive Components Division, Electrical and Fuel Handling Division, Glass Division and Chassis Division.
The new unit has more than 75,000 hourly and salaried workers at plants, administrative offices, and engineering and technical centers in 19 countries on four continents.

The group had combined revenues of more than $14 billion and assets of more than $4 billion in 1995. Newly appointed Vice Chairman Edward Hagenlocker will oversee the organization as part of his new duties.

Trotman said there is not expected to be a significant change in headcount as a result of the new structure. He said he envisions the new unit increasing its percentage of sales to non-Ford automotive customers as a way of boosting its own competitive performance and contributing to Ford Motor's total revenues.

The vast majority of products now made by the four businesses is used by other Ford divisions, a company spokeswoman said. About five percent of the new group's revenues currently come from non-Ford automakers.

Trotman said the new structure will "expose the operations nakedly -- for want of a better word -- to the whims of competition, to really make them much more of an arms' length supplier of components to the automotive business than they are today."

Specifically, Trotman mentioned the Glass Division as one business that could be targeted for selling. Ford had previously tried to sell the division, arguing it is difficult for it to be competitive with large volume glass producers.
Trotman said the automaker's new three-year labor agreement with the United Auto Workers union provides flexibility to Ford as it seeks to increase the efficiency of the parts businesses.
Although the company guaranteed 95 percent of its current UAW workforce, the company can pay a lower wage if it wants to enter a new business that it is not currently involved in.
Also, the company can count three of the lower-paid, new- businesses workers for every two higher-paid UAW workers who retire in computing the 95 percent level.
